A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same elicitation study. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support comparison. Internal numerical inconsistencies affect particular findings, not material completeness.

before.justification: v1 reports original WMDP and APPS experiments evaluating elicitation techniques on password-locked and circuit-broken language models, including quantitative results and appendix analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds MMLU experiments and comparisons involving supervised fine-tuning of the original models.

M1.justification: Password-locking, subsequent circuit-breaking, activation losses, and the modified coefficient scheduler are unchanged. The existing prompting, steering, and fine-tuning procedures are extended to MMLU without introducing a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: Sections 3.1 and 4.2 add MMLU training and evaluation, extending multiple-choice coverage from hazardous knowledge to general knowledge and problem solving across STEM, humanities, and social sciences. WMDP and APPS remain. Gemma's WMDP experiments were already present in v1.

E2.justification: New Table 3 adds fine-tuned original models as controls alongside fine-tuned model organisms. v1 reported original-model performance but lacked these fine-tuned-original comparisons. The established prompting, steering, anti-refusal, and supervised fine-tuning comparator set otherwise remains.

E3.justification: The added MMLU experiments use 1,402 samples with the existing 50/10/25/5/10 partition scheme and benchmark-specific circuit-breaking and fine-tuning settings in Tables 8 and 12. Table 3 also introduces original-model fine-tuning controls. Previously stated WMDP and APPS protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 3 adds a before-and-after fine-tuning comparison of original models and model organisms, providing a control for examining whether performance differences are specific to elicitation. Existing shot-count analyses, multi-turn tests, and conversation case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point accuracies without repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional results and parsing-error caveat do not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial MMLU results in Table 2 and Figures 5–6, plus original-model fine-tuning scores in Table 3. Figure 3 changes Gemma's circuit-broken WMDP regular-prompt score from 30.0% to 14.9% and its supervised fine-tuning score from 60% to 62%. However, Table 1 retains 30.0%, leaving an unresolved discrepancy. Existing detailed WMDP and APPS tables otherwise retain their values.

T1.justification: The capability definitions, password-locking formulation, circuit-breaking losses, and scheduler equations are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: circuit-broken model organisms, comparison of elicitation techniques, benefits of combining techniques, and preference for fine-tuning when available. MMLU supplies additional evidence without redefining these claims.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 adds interpretations of benchmark-dependent steering effectiveness and MMLU-specific circuit-breaking failures, extending the existing discussion of training fragility. It also cautions that answer parsing may underestimate Mistral anti-refusal performance. Future work adds comparison with random-noise fine-tuning to investigate anti-refusal mechanisms.

D1.justification: Tables 8 and 12 document MMLU circuit-breaking parameters and supervised fine-tuning learning rates, while prompting and steering details explicitly extend to MMLU. The abstract changes the advertised code/results location from an anonymous mirror to a named GitHub repository. Existing implementation and hardware details are retained.

R1.justification: Related work adds Che et al.'s model-tampering study and connects elicitation to white-box attacks on models after unlearning. The bibliography lists this same work twice as 2025a and 2025b. The broader research positioning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section organization are retained. v3 inserts an MMLU results subsection, expands future work, adds an author and acknowledgement/contribution statements, and moves the impact statement from the appendix before the references. These are localized changes rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the workflow diagram and restyles the main result plots, changing colors and legends, removing password-locking overlay markers from Figure 3, and placing both WMDP plots together. New MMLU plots and comparative and hyperparameter tables substantially expand the quantitative presentation.

improvement.justification: MMLU provides useful evidence about generalization beyond hazardous knowledge and exposes model-specific failures, while Table 3's original-model fine-tuning controls improve assessment of training effects. These strengthen the empirical account without changing the core method. The gain is limited by reporting inconsistencies, particularly Figure 3's new 14.9% Gemma baseline conflicting with Table 1's retained 30.0%.
